Adult female Buff-throated saltators attain an ultimate wet body weight of approximately 50 grams [Wwi = approximately 50 grams], a figure that aligns closely with the upper end of the 47 to 50 gram range reported for conspecifics, whereas adult males are conspicuously lighter, reaching a maximum of around 45 grams [Wwi = around 45 grams] and typically falling within a 43 to 45 gram interval. This modest sexual size dimorphism is consistent with patterns observed among other members of the genus Saltator, where males are frequently described as the slightly smaller sex. At hatching, nestlings emerge with an initial wet weight of nearly 5.75 grams [Ww0 = nearly 5.75 grams], a value that reflects the limited yolk reserves typical of altricial passerine chicks. This neonatal mass represents only a small fraction of the adult weight, underscoring the substantial growth trajectory that must be completed during the nestling period before the young can achieve independence.

When eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], the incubation period proceeds to completion, and the age at hatching has been recorded at approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days]. This relatively brief embryonic development is characteristic of many Neotropical passerines inhabiting warm, lowland environments, where elevated nest temperatures accelerate ontogenetic processes. During the post-hatching phase, thermoregulatory demands shift considerably, and the nestlings are brooded intensively by both parents. After they emerge from the egg, the chicks remain entirely dependent on parental provisioning for nourishment, with their body temperature closely tracking the ambient conditions until the plumage develops sufficiently to provide insulation. The duration of incubation at 38 °C [T = 38 °C] appears to be finely tuned to the thermal regime of the nest microhabitat, and deviations from this temperature can extend or shorten the hatching period.

Under the thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic period of this species, typically around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental landmarks unfolds. Fledging, marked by the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early fledging age suggests a strong selective pressure to minimize the duration of nest vulnerability, given the high predation rates that affect open-cup nests in tropical forests. Shortly after this milestone, the juveniles begin to forage independently, although they may continue to receive occasional food from the parents for several additional days. The rapid transition from a sedentary nestling to a mobile fledgling is accompanied by significant changes in muscle mass, feather development, and coordination. Field observations indicate that the post-fledging period is a critical window during which mortality rates are elevated, as the young birds must learn to identify suitable food items and avoid predators without the full protection of the nest.

Sexual maturation in the Buff-throated saltator is attained at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] when measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], an interval that corresponds to the completion of the juvenile molt and the acquisition of definitive adult plumage. This timing indicates that reproductive development progresses relatively rapidly in this species compared to many temperate-zone passerines, which often delay puberty until the following breeding season. However, the onset of physiological capability does not coincide immediately with actual breeding activity. Instead, there is a substantial lag before first reproduction, with first breeding events typically occurring at 1.5 years after hatching [tR = 1.5 years after hatching] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay is thought to reflect the time required for young birds to establish territories, acquire foraging skills, and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of egg production and nestling care.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Buff-throated saltator under field conditions reaches approximately 9.7 years [am = approximately 9.7 years], a value that is notably long for a passerine of this body size and that has been documented at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Reproductive output is characterized by a modest clutch size and a restricted breeding season; females typically lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch] and produce about 2.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = about 2.5 clutches per year], which together yield a daily reproductive rate that supports stable population recruitment despite the small brood size. Basal metabolic rate, measured as resting oxygen consumption, reaches 98.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 98.5 milliliters per hour] at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], reflecting the elevated energetic costs associated with endothermy in a warm but variable tropical environment. This value falls within the range reported for other Saltator species and underscores the relatively slow life-history pace that distinguishes this Neotropical passerine from its temperate counterparts.
